Republican Anti-Flock Bill Might Ban All Automated Traffic Enforcement

CA
By Chloe Adams Car Culture & Restomod Editor • via Jalopnik Wire
⚡ Visual Story
Source & Photography: Jalopnik Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • CHLOE ADAMS Car Culture & Restomod Editor

Heritage Preservation vs Modern Performance

Automotive passion is increasingly defined by the synthesis of analog soul and contemporary engineering. This coverage from Jalopnik illustrates how bespoke builders, private collectors, and restomod artists are preserving the golden eras of internal combustion while adopting carbon fiber composites and precision craftsmanship.

Big Picture: Auction hammer prices and enthusiast demand indicate sustained historical appreciation for rare, analog driver's vehicles.

The rise of mass automated license-plate-reader surveillance in recent years, its reckless implementation and rampant abuse by rank-and-file police officers have quickly become unacceptable to many Americans . So it's perhaps unsurprising that U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie and six co-sponsors introduced the Flock-Off Act in Congress last month. The bill proposed withdrawing all federal funding from any municipality with "covered camera system" operator contracts, not just with Flock. The bill's language would also cover automated speed and red light cameras.

📌 The Core Development

Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary in May, said his bill aims to prevent law enforcement from surveilling "law-abiding citizens." Despite good intentions, though, the lawmakers behind the Flock-Off Act seemingly didn't comprehend the ramifications of its catch-all wording. The only Democratic co-sponsor of the bill, California Rep. Ro Khanna, told Streetsblog , "I'm for speed and red light cameras. You don't have speed and red light cameras being abused by police officers." Currently, the Flock-Off Act exempts only cameras used for tolling and cameras placed within a mile of the country's northern and southern borders.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

Flock's deployment of automated license-plate-reading cameras is fundamentally different from speed and red light cameras. The mass surveillance network captures every license plate that passes, creating a database accessible to virtually every Flock customer. Speed and red light cameras only trigger when they detect an infraction beyond a set threshold. This trigger also makes the cameras serve as a deterrent to drivers breaking the law. According to the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency , speeding dropped by 84% after it first deployed speed cameras in 2025. These cameras also eliminate the need for most traffic stops, which can lead to deadly police interactions either during the stop or in a high-speed pursuit.
